stem: GuessingGame has NO Console calls anywhere. The payoff:
options: The same rules work in a console, a web page OR a test - and the COMPUTER can play it
explanation: Separating rules from I/O is the module's central habit. It is also what lets binary search drive the game automatically.

stem: Guess() throwing InvalidOperationException when IsOver is true demonstrates:
options: The object ENFORCING its own rules - a finished game refuses more guesses (2.4, 4.7's 'wrong time')
explanation: The state machine protects itself. Meanwhile an out-of-range guess RETURNS a value - bad input is expected, not exceptional.

options: BINARY SEARCH - 'too low/high' is exactly the comparison it needs (5.2)
explanation: Higher/lower IS the comparison; halving the range is optimal. The project turns 5.2 into a playable strategy.

stem: Playing every secret 1-100, binary search's WORST case is:
explanation: The project proves 5.1's theory empirically: ~5.8 average and 7 worst, against linear's 50.5 average.

stem: GuessResult (TooLow/TooHigh/Correct/OutOfRange) as an enum rather than strings gives:
options: Compile-checked results a switch can exhaust - no misspelled "to low" (2.8, 1.5)
explanation: Enums make the possible outcomes explicit and the switch complete. Magic strings cannot be misspelled if they do not exist.

stem: An out-of-range guess returns OutOfRange WITHOUT incrementing Attempts because:
options: It was not a real guess - a design decision that the rules class owns, not the UI
explanation: The game defines what counts as an attempt - a rule living with its data, testable in isolation.

stem: 'You think of a number, the computer guesses' reuses:
options: The SAME binary-search brain already written - only the roles swap
explanation: Because rules and strategy are separate, the playing logic transplants directly. Good separation pays extension dividends.

stem: The interactive front end stays crash-proof using:
options: while(true) + TryParse - the 1.3 validation loop; the rules class handles the rest
explanation: The thin console layer is the 1.3 pattern; every game rule is already enforced by the class.

stem: Because the game has no Console dependency, you can test it by:
options: Calling Guess() and asserting on the returned enum and Attempts - no I/O involved
explanation: A pure rules object is trivially testable - the recurring reward of keeping logic away from I/O.

stem: Extending the range to 1-1,000,000, the worst-case optimal guesses become:
explanation: log2 scaling means a million-wide range costs 20, a billion costs 30. The power of halving, one last time.
